Hessian Nilpotent Polynomials and the Jacobian Conjecture

Wenhua Zhao
Abstract.

Let z=(z1,⋯,zn)z=(z_{1},\cdots,z_{n}) and Δ=∑i=1n∂2∂zi2\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial z^{2}_{i}} the Laplace operator. The main goal of the paper is to show that the well-known Jacobian conjecture without any additional conditions is equivalent to the following what we call vanishing conjecture: for any homogeneous polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d=4d=4, if Δm​Pm​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1, then Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 when m>>0m>>0, or equivalently, Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 when m>32​(3n−2−1)m>\frac{3}{2}(3^{n-2}-1). It is also shown in this paper that the condition Δm​Pm​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)=0 (m≥1m\geq 1) above is equivalent to the condition that P⁡(z)P(z) is Hessian nilpotent, i.e. the Hessian matrix Hes ​P​(z)=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}P(z)=(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}) is nilpotent. The goal is achieved by using the recent breakthrough work of M. de Bondt, A. van den Essen [BE1] and various results obtained in this paper on Hessian nilpotent polynomials. Some further results on Hessian nilpotent polynomials and the vanishing conjecture above are also derived.

Key words and phrases: 
Hessian nilpotent polynomials, Deformed inversion pairs, the Heat equation, harmonic polynomials, the Jacobian conjecture.

1. Introduction

Let z=(z1,z2,⋯,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\cdots,z_{n}) and F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) be a formal map from ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} to ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with o⁡(H⁡(z))≥2o(H(z))\geq 2 and G⁡(z)G(z) the formal inverse map of F⁡(z)F(z). The well-known Jacobian conjecture first proposed by Keller [Ke] in 1939 claims that, if F⁡(z)F(z) is a polynomial map with the Jacobian j​(F)​(z)=1j(F)(z)=1, the inverse map G⁡(z)G(z) must also be a polynomial map. Despite intense study from mathematicians in more than half a century, the conjecture is still wide open even for the case n=2n=2. In 1998, S. Smale [S] included the Jacobian conjecture in his list of 1818 important mathematical problems for 2121st century. For more history and known results on the Jacobian conjecture, see [BCW], [E] and references there. Recently, M. de Bondt and A. van den Essen [BE1] (Also see G. Meng [M]) have made a breakthrough on the Jacobian conjecture. They reduced the Jacobian conjecture to polynomial maps F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) with H⁡(z)=∇P​(z)=(∂P∂z1,∂P∂z2,⋯,∂P∂zn)H(z)=\nabla P(z)=(\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{1}},\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{2}},\cdots,\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{n}}) for some polynomials P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z]. In this paper, we will refer to this reduction as the gradient reduction and the condition H​(z)=∇P​(z)H(z)=\nabla P(z) for some P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] as the gradient condition. Note that, by Poincaré lemma, a formal map F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) with o⁡(H⁡(z))≥2o(H(z))\geq 2 satisfies the gradient condition if and only if its Jacobian matrix J​F​(z)JF(z) is symmetric. Following the terminology in [BE1], we also call the formal maps satisfying the gradient condition symmetric formal maps.

For further discussion, let us fix the following notions. A power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] is said to be HN (Hessian nilpotent) if its Hessian matrix Hes ​P​(z)=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}P(z)=(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}) is nilpotent. Let tt be a formal parameter which commutes with zz. The deformed inversion pair Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 is the unique power series Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z,t]]Q_{t}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z,t]] with o⁡(Qt​(z))≥2o(Q_{t}(z))\geq 2 such that the formal map G(z)=z+t∇Qt(z)G(z)=z+t\nabla Q_{t}(z) is the inverse map of F(z)=z−t∇P(z)F(z)=z-t\nabla P(z). Recently, G. Meng [M] and D. Wright [Wr1] have derived a tree expansion formula for the inverse map G⁡(z)G(z) of F​(z)=Ft=1​(z)F(z)=F_{t=1}(z). In [Z2], by studying the PDE satisfied by the deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z), the author has derived a recurrent formula and a binary rooted tree expansion formula for the deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z). Furthermore, some close relationships among the deformed inversion pairs, the Legendre transform, the inviscid Burgers’ equations and the Jacobian conjecture are also clarified in [Z2]. For some other recent results on symmetric polynomial or formal maps, see [BE1]–[BE5], [EW], [M], [Wr1], [Wr2] and [Z2].

In this paper, we will use some general results in [Z2] to study HNS (Hessian nilpotent power series) P⁡(z)P(z) and their deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z). Furthermore, by using the gradient reduction in [BE1] and various results derived in this paper on HN polynomials, we will show that the Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to what we call vanishing conjectures of homogeneous HN polynomials. (See the discussion below.) We first derive the PDE’s satisfied by Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z), Δk​Qtm\Delta^{k}Q_{t}^{m} (k,m≥1)(k,m\geq 1) and exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))\exp(sQ_{t}(z)) (s∈ℂ×)(s\in{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}), where Δ=∑i=1n∂2∂zi2\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial z^{2}_{i}} is the Laplace operator. In particular, we show in Theorem 3.2 that exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))\exp(sQ_{t}(z)) (s∈ℂ×)(s\in{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}) is the unique power series solution of the Cauchy problem of the Heat equation with the initial condition exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))|t=0=exp⁡(s​P​(z))\left.\exp(sQ_{t}(z))\right|_{t=0}=\exp(sP(z)). We then derive a uniform formula (See Theorem 3.4.) for the powers Qtk​(z)Q_{t}^{k}(z) (k≥1)(k\geq 1) of the deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of HNS P⁡(z)P(z). We also prove a general theorem, Theorem 4.1, on a relationship between {Tr Hesm​(P⁡(z))|m≥1}\{\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes}^{m}(P(z))|m\geq 1\} and {Δm​Pm​(z)|m≥1}\{\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)|m\geq 1\} for any power series P⁡(z)P(z). From this theorem, we show in Theorem 4.3 that, for any formal power series P⁡(z)P(z), it is HN if and only if Δm​Pm​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1, or equivalently, Δm​Pm​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)=0 for any 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n. Finally, we prove some identities, vanishing properties and isotropic properties of {ΔkPm(z)|m,k≥0}\{\Delta^{k}P^{m}(z)|m,k\geq 0\} for HNS or HNP’s (Hessian nilpotent polynomials) P⁡(z)P(z). Some close relationships of the deformed pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of HNS or HNP’s P⁡(z)P(z) with the Heat equation and the Jacobian conjecture are also clarified. In particular, we show that the Jacobian conjecture without any additional conditions is equivalent to the following vanishing conjectures: for any HNP P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d=4d=4, Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 for m>>0m>>0, or more precisely, for all m>32​(3n−2−1)m>\frac{3}{2}(3^{n-2}-1).

One remark is that, due to the identity Tr Hes ​(P)=Δ​P\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes\,}(P)=\Delta P, any HNS P⁡(z)P(z) is automatically harmonic, i.e. Δ​P​(z)=0\Delta P(z)=0. Note that harmonic polynomials (See [ABR], [H] and [T].) are among the most classical objects in mathematics and have been very well studied. The classical study on harmonic polynomials started from Legendre, Laplace, Jacobi in the late eighteen century. The modern generalizations of harmonic polynomials, namely, spherical functions, were first studied by Cartan and Weyl in the 1930’s and later by Gelfand, Harish-Chandra, etc. It is quite surprising to see that, first, HNP’s as a family of very special harmonic polynomials are closely related with the notorious Jacobian conjecture. Secondly, it seems that HNP’s have been overlooked and have not been studied until the recent work of M. de Bondt, A. van den Essen [BE1] and G. Meng [M]. Besides the connections with the Jacobian conjecture discussed above, another interesting aspect of HNP’s is their connection with the classical inviscid Burgers’ equation in Diffusion theory and also the Heat equation. Actually, the vanishing conjecture above is also equivalent to saying that the power series solutions of certain Cauchy problems of the inviscid Burgers’ equation and the Heat equation must be polynomials and the exponentials of polynomials, respectively. (See discussion in Section 44 in [Z2] and Conjecture 3.3 in this paper.) Considering the connections of HNP’s with the classical objects described above, we believe that HNP’s deserve much more attentions from mathematicians.

Considering the length of this paper, we give the following detailed arrangement description. In Section 2, we first fix some notation and definitions that are needed throughout the rest of this paper. We then briefly recall certain results obtained in [Z2] and prove some preliminary results including the PDE (See Corollary 2.7) satisfied by Δk​Qtm\Delta^{k}Q_{t}^{m} (k,m≥1)(k,m\geq 1) for the deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of any power series P⁡(z)P(z). In Section 3, for any HNS P⁡(z)P(z) and its deformed inversion pair Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z), we derive the PDE’s satisfied by Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) and exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))\exp(sQ_{t}(z)) (s∈ℂ×)(s\in{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}), from which we derive with two different proofs a uniform formula Eq. (3.8) for Qtk​(z)Q_{t}^{k}(z) (k≥1)(k\geq 1). In Section 4, we prove a general theorem, Theorem 4.1, on a relationship between {Tr Hesm​(P⁡(z))|m≥1}\{\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes}^{m}(P(z))|m\geq 1\} and {Δm​Pm​(z)|m≥1}\{\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)|m\geq 1\} for the universal formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2. From this theorem, we deduce a criterion in Theorem 4.3 for the Hessian nilpotency of a formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) in terms of certain vanishing properties of {Δm​Pm​(z)|m≥1}\{\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)|m\geq 1\}. In Section 5.1, by using a fundamental theorem of harmonic polynomials (See Theorem 5.2), we derive a criterion in Proposition 5.3 for Hessian nilpotency of homogeneous harmonic polynomials. In Section 5.2, we give constructions for some HNP’s and HNS. In Section 6, by using some of the main results in the previous sections, we prove more properties of HNS or HNP’s P⁡(z)P(z). We prove in Proposition 6.1 an identity and in Theorem 6.2 an equivalence of certain vanishing properties of {ΔkPm(z)|k,m≥1}\{\Delta^{k}P^{m}(z)|k,m\geq 1\} for HNS P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]. In Theorem 6.3, we show some isotropic properties for homogeneous HNP’s. In Section 7, we discuss some applications to the Jacobian conjecture. We formulate the vanishing conjecture, Conjecture 7.1, for (not necessary homogeneous) HNP’s and the homogeneous vanishing conjecture, Conjecture 7.3, for homogeneous HNP’s. We show in Proposition 7.4 that both conjectures above are equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture.

Finally, some remarks on this paper are as follows. First, for convenience, we will fix ℂ{\mathbb{C}} as our base field. But, all results, formulas as well as their proofs (except the 1st proof of Theorem 3.4) obtained in this paper hold or work equally well if one replace ℂ{\mathbb{C}} by any ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra. Secondly, we will not restrict our study just on HNP’s. Instead, we will formulate and prove results for HN formal power series whenever they hold in this general setting. Thirdly, for any HNP’s or locally convergent HNS P⁡(z)P(z), all formal power series involved in this paper are locally convergent. This can be seen either from the fact that any local analytic map with non-zero Jacobian at the origin has a locally convergent inverse, or from the well-known Cauchy-Kowaleskaya theorem (See [R], for example.)

2. Deformed Inversion Pairs of Formal Power Series

In this section, we first fix some notation and definitions that are needed in this paper. We then briefly recall certain results obtained in [Z2] and prove some preliminary results.

2.1. Notation and Conventions

Once and for all, we fix the following notation and conventions.

  1. (1)

    We fix n≥1n\geq 1 and set z=(z1,z2,⋯,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\cdots,z_{n}). For any ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra kk, we denote by k⁡[z]k[z] (resp. k⁡[[z]]k[[z]]) the polynomial algebra (resp. formal power series algebra) over kk in ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

  2. (2)

    For any ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra kk, by a formal map F⁡(z)F(z) from knk^{n} to knk^{n}, we simply mean F⁡(z)=(F1​(z),F2​(z),⋯,Fn​(z))F(z)=(F_{1}(z),F_{2}(z),\cdots,F_{n}(z)) with Fi​(z)∈k​[[z]]F_{i}(z)\in k[[z]] (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). We denote by J⁡(F)J(F) and j⁡(F)j(F) the Jacobian matrix and the Jacobian of F⁡(z)F(z), respectively.

  3. (3)

    We denote by Δ\Delta the Laplace operator ∑i=1n∂2∂zi2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial z_{i}^{2}}. Note that, a polynomial or formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) is said to be harmonic if Δ​P=0\Delta P=0.

  4. (4)

    For any k≥1k\geq 1 and U⁡(z)=(U1​(z),U2​(z),⋯,Uk​(z))∈ℂ​[[z]]×kU(z)=(U_{1}(z),U_{2}(z),\cdots,U_{k}(z))\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]^{\times k}, we set

    o⁡(U⁡(z))=min1≤i≤k⁡o⁡(Ui​(z))\displaystyle o(U(z))=\min_{1\leq i\leq k}o(U_{i}(z))

    and, when U⁡(z)∈ℂ​[z]×kU(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z]^{\times k},

    deg⁡U⁡(z)=max1≤i≤k⁡deg⁡Ui​(z).\displaystyle\deg U(z)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\deg U_{i}(z).

    For any Ut​(z)∈ℂ⁡[t]​[[z]]×k​ or ​ℂ​[[z,t]]×kU_{t}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[t][[z]]^{\times k}\text{ or }{\mathbb{C}}[[z,t]]^{\times k} (k≥1k\geq 1) for some formal parameter tt, the notation o​(Ut​(z))o(U_{t}(z)) and deg⁡Ut​(z)\deg U_{t}(z) always stand for the order and the degree of Ut​(z)U_{t}(z) with respect to zz, respectively.

  5. (5)

    For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]], we denote by ∇P​(z)\nabla P(z) the gradient of P⁡(z)P(z), i.e. ∇P=(∂P∂z1,∂P∂z2,⋯,∂P∂zn)\nabla P=(\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{1}},\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{2}},\cdots,\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{n}}). We denote by Hes ​(P)​(z)\text{Hes\,}(P)(z) the Hessian matrix of P⁡(z)P(z), i.e. Hes ​(P)​(z)=(∂2P⁡(z)∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}(P)(z)=(\frac{\partial^{2}P(z)}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}).

  6. (6)

    All nn-vectors in this paper are supposed to be column vectors unless stated otherwise. For any vector or matrix UU, we denote by UtU^{t} its transpose. The standard ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear form of nn-vectors is denoted by <⋅,⋅><\cdot,\cdot>.

The following lemma will be very useful in our later arguments.

Lemma 2.1.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] and m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(2.1) Δ​Pm+1​(z)=(m+1)​Pm​Δ​P+m⁡(m+1)​Pm−1​<∇P,∇P>\displaystyle\Delta P^{m+1}(z)=(m+1)P^{m}\Delta P+m(m+1)P^{m-1}<\nabla P,\nabla P>

or

(2.2) Pm−1​<∇P,∇P>=1m⁡(m+1)​(Δ​Pm+1−(m+1)​Pm​Δ​P).\displaystyle P^{m-1}<\nabla P,\nabla P>=\frac{1}{m(m+1)}\left(\Delta P^{m+1}-(m+1)P^{m}\Delta P\right).

Furthermore, when P⁡(z)P(z) is harmonic, we have

(2.3) Pm−1​Δ​P2=2m⁡(m+1)​Δ​Pm+1.\displaystyle P^{m-1}\Delta P^{2}=\frac{2}{m(m+1)}\Delta P^{m+1}.

Proof:  Consider

Δ​Pm+1\displaystyle\Delta P^{m+1} =∑i=1n∂∂zi​∂∂zi​Pm+1\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}P^{m+1}
=(m+1)​∑i=1n∂∂zi​(Pm​∂P∂zi)\displaystyle=(m+1)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}(P^{m}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}})
=(m+1)​∑i=1nPm​∂2P∂zi2+m⁡(m+1)​∑i=1nPm−1​∂P∂zi​∂P∂zi\displaystyle=(m+1)\sum_{i=1}^{n}P^{m}\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}^{2}}+m(m+1)\sum_{i=1}^{n}P^{m-1}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}
=(m+1)​Pm​Δ​P+m⁡(m+1)​<∇P,∇P>​Pm−1.\displaystyle=(m+1)P^{m}\Delta P+m(m+1)<\nabla P,\nabla P>P^{m-1}.

Hence, we get Eq. (2.1) and (2.2).

Now suppose that P⁡(z)P(z) is harmonic, i.e. Δ​P=0\Delta P=0. By Eq. (2.1) with m=1m=1, we have Δ​P2=2​<∇P,∇P>\Delta P^{2}=2<\nabla P,\nabla P> or <∇P,∇P>=12​Δ​P2<\nabla P,\nabla P>=\frac{1}{2}\Delta P^{2}. It is easy to see that, in this case, Eq. (2.3) follows directly from Eq. (2.2).  □\Box

2.2. Deformed Inversion Pairs of Formal Power Series

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, we set F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z). It is shown in §​1.1\lx@sectionsign 1.1 in [M] (Also see Lemma 3.13.1 in [Z2].) that there is a unique Q⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]Q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(Q⁡(z))≥2o(Q(z))\geq 2 such that the formal inverse of F⁡(z)F(z) is given by G​(z)=z+∇Q​(z)G(z)=z+\nabla Q(z). We call Q⁡(z)Q(z) the inversion pair of P⁡(z)P(z). Furthermore, following the arguments in [Z1] and [Z2], we also consider the deformation Ft(z)=z−t∇P(z)F_{t}(z)=z-t\nabla P(z) of F⁡(z)F(z), where tt is a formal parameter which commutes with variables ziz_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). By Lemma 3.13.1 in [Z2], we know that there exists a unique Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z,t]]Q_{t}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z,t]] with o⁡(Qt​(z))≥2o(Q_{t}(z))\geq 2 such that the formal inverse Gt​(z)G_{t}(z) of Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) is given by Gt(z)=z+t∇Qt(z)G_{t}(z)=z+t\nabla Q_{t}(z). Note that, when o⁡(P⁡(z))≥3o(P(z))\geq 3, we actually have Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[t]​[[z]]Q_{t}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[t][[z]] and Qt=1​(z)=Q​(z)Q_{t=1}(z)=Q(z). In general, t​Qt​(z)tQ_{t}(z) is nothing but the inversion pair of t​P​(z)tP(z) over the ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra ℂ⁡[[t]]{\mathbb{C}}[[t]]. Another way to look at the inversion pair is as follows. Set U⁡(z)=12​∑i=1nzi2−P⁡(z)U(z)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}-P(z) and V⁡(z)=12​∑i=1nzi2+Q⁡(z)V(z)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}+Q(z), then V⁡(z)V(z) is exactly the Legendre transform (See [Ar], [M] and [Z2].) of the formal power series U⁡(z)U(z).

Definition 2.2.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z,t]]Q_{t}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z,t]] defined above is called the deformed inversion pair of P⁡(z)P(z).

Another important definition is the following.

Definition 2.3.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]], we say P⁡(z)P(z) is HN ((Hessian nilpotent)) if its Hessian matrix Hes ​(P)=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}(P)=\left(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}\right) is nilpotent.

Remark 2.4.

Note that, Tr Hes ​(P)=Δ​P\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes\,}(P)=\Delta P for any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]. Hence any HN formal power series is harmonic. But the converse is not true. For some examples of HNP’s and HNS, see Subsection 5.2.

Throughout the rest of this paper, for any formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]], we will fix the notation F⁡(z)F(z), Ft​(z)F_{t}(z), G⁡(z)G(z), Gt​(z)G_{t}(z), Q⁡(z)Q(z) and Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) defined above unless stated otherwise. We will use the short words HNS and HNP for “HN power series” and “HN polynomial”, respectively. Furthermore, we also define a sequence of formal power series {Q[m]​(z)|m≥1}\{Q_{[m]}(z)|m\geq 1\} by writing

(2.4) Qt​(z)=∑m=1∞tm−1​Q[m]​(z).\displaystyle Q_{t}(z)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}t^{m-1}Q_{[m]}(z).
Lemma 2.5.

For any formal power series P⁡(z)P(z), we have

  1. (a)

3. Deformed Inversion Pairs of HN Power Series

In this section, we study deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of HNS (Hessian Nilpotent Formal Power Series) P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]. We first derive the PDE’s satisfied by Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) and exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))\exp(sQ_{t}(z)) (s∈ℂ×)(s\in{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}). We then discuss some relationships among deformed inversion pairs, the Heat equation and the Jacobian conjecture. Note that similar relationships among deformed inversion pairs of formal power series (not necessarily HN), the inviscid Burgers’ equations and the Jacobian conjecture have been discussed in [Z2]. Finally, we derive with two different proofs a uniform non-recurrent formula (See Eq. (3.8).) for Qtk​(z)Q_{t}^{k}(z) (k≥1)(k\geq 1).

Theorem 3.1.

For any Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z,t]]Q_{t}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z,t]] with o⁡(Qt​(z))≥2o(Q_{t}(z))\geq 2 and HNS P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, the following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) is the deformed inversion pair of P⁡(z)P(z).

  2. (2)

    Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) is the unique power series solution of the following Cauchy problem of PDE.

    (3.1) {∂Qt​(z)∂t=14​Δ​Qt2,Qt=0​(z)=P⁡(z).\displaystyle\begin{cases}\frac{\partial Q_{t}(z)}{\partial t}&=\frac{1}{4}\Delta Q_{t}^{2},\\ Q_{t=0}(z)&=P(z).\end{cases}

Furthermore, we have the following recurrent formula.

(3.2) Q[1]​(z)\displaystyle Q_{[1]}(z) =P⁡(z),\displaystyle=P(z),
(3.3) Q[m]​(z)\displaystyle Q_{[m]}(z) =14​(m−1)​Δ​∑k,l≥1k+l=mQ[k]​(z)​Q[l]​(z)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4(m-1)}\Delta\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,l\geq 1\\ k+l=m\end{subarray}}Q_{[k]}(z)Q_{[l]}(z)

for any m≥2m\geq 2.

Proof:  First, by Lemma 2.5, (b)(b), we have Δ​Qt​(z)=0\Delta Q_{t}(z)=0. Therefore, for any m≥1m\geq 1, Q[m]​(z)Q_{[m]}(z) is harmonic. Secondly, for any harmonic formal power series U⁡(z),U(z),V(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]], it is easy to check that we have

(3.4) Δ⁡(U​V)=2​<∇U,∇V>.\displaystyle\Delta(UV)=2<\nabla U,\nabla V>.

By using the facts above, it is easy to see that the implication (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2) and also the recurrent formulas Eq. (3.2), (3.3) follow directly from Theorem 2.6.

To see (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1), we denote by Q~t​(z)\widetilde{Q}_{t}(z) the deformed inversion pair of P⁡(z)P(z). By the fact proved above, we know that Q~t​(z)\widetilde{Q}_{t}(z) also satisfies Eq. (3.1). Since the power series solution of the Cauchy problem Eq. (3.1) is unique, which is given recursively by Eq. (3.2) and (3.3), we have Q~t​(z)=Qt​(z)\widetilde{Q}_{t}(z)=Q_{t}(z). Therefore (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1) also holds.  □\Box

A relation of deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of HNS P⁡(z)P(z) with the Heat equation is given by the following theorem.

Theorem 3.2.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] be HN with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 and Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) its deformed inversion pair. For any non-zero s∈ℂs\in{\mathbb{C}}, set

Ut,s​(z)=exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))=∑k=0∞sk​Qtk​(z)k!.\displaystyle U_{t,s}(z)=\exp(sQ_{t}(z))=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{s^{k}Q_{t}^{k}(z)}{k!}.

Then, Ut,s​(z)U_{t,s}(z) is the unique formal power series solution of the following Cauchy problem of the Heat equation.

(3.5) {∂Ut,s∂t​(z)=12​s​Δ​Ut,s​(z),Ut=0,s​(z)=exp⁡(s​P​(z)).\displaystyle\begin{cases}\frac{\partial U_{t,s}}{\partial t}(z)&=\frac{1}{2s}\Delta U_{t,s}(z),\\ U_{t=0,s}(z)&=\exp(sP(z)).\end{cases}

Proof:  The uniqueness can be proved by viewing Ut,s​(z)U_{t,s}(z) as a power series in tt with coefficients in ℂ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] and showing that the coefficients of tkt^{k} (k≥1)(k\geq 1) are recurrently determined by the coefficient of t0t^{0} which is Ut=0,s​(z)=exp⁡(s​P​(z))U_{t=0,s}(z)=\exp(sP(z)). We skip the details here. For a similar argument, see the proof of Proposition 2.52.5 in [Z2]. Note that, when P⁡(z)P(z) is locally convergent, Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) and exp⁡(s​Qt​(z))\exp(sQ_{t}(z)) (s∈ℂ×)(s\in{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}) are locally convergent. Then the uniqueness in this case also follows from the Cauchy-Kowaleskaya theorem (See [R]) in PDE.

Now we show that Ut,s​(z)U_{t,s}(z) satisfies Eq. (3.5). First note that, the initial condition in Eq. (3.5) follows immediately from the one in Eq. (2.8). Secondly, by Lemma 2.5, (b)(b), we have Δ​Qt​(z)=0\Delta Q_{t}(z)=0.

Consider

(3.6) ∂Ut,s∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial U_{t,s}}{\partial t} =∂exp⁡(s​Qt)∂t\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\exp(sQ_{t})}{\partial t}
=s​exp⁡(s​Qt)​∂Qt∂t\displaystyle=s\exp(sQ_{t})\frac{\partial Q_{t}}{\partial t}
Applying Eq. (2.8):
=s2​Ut,s​<∇Qt,∇Qt>.\displaystyle=\frac{s}{2}U_{t,s}<\nabla Q_{t},\nabla Q_{t}>.

On the other hand, we have

(3.7) Δ​Ut,s\displaystyle\Delta U_{t,s} =∑i=1n∂∂zi​∂∂zi​es​Qt\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}e^{sQ_{t}}
=s​∑i=1n∂∂zi​(∂Qt∂zi​es​Qt)\displaystyle=s\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}(\frac{\partial Q_{t}}{\partial z_{i}}e^{sQ_{t}})
Using the fact that Δ​Qt=0\Delta Q_{t}=0:
=s2​∑i=1n∂Qt∂zi​∂Qt∂zi​es​Qt\displaystyle=s^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial Q_{t}}{\partial z_{i}}\frac{\partial Q_{t}}{\partial z_{i}}e^{sQ_{t}}
=s2​Us,t​<∇Qt,∇Qt>.\displaystyle=s^{2}U_{s,t}<\nabla Q_{t},\nabla Q_{t}>.

By combining Eq. (3.6) and (3.7), we see that Ut,s​(z)U_{t,s}(z) does satisfy the PDE in Eq. (3.5).  □\Box

By combining the gradient reduction in [BE1], [M] and the homogeneous reduction in [BCW], [Y] on the Jacobian conjecture, we see that the Jacobian conjecture can be reduced to polynomial maps F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) with P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] homogeneous of degree d=4d=4. By Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, it is easy to see that the Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to the following conjecture.

Conjecture 3.3.

For any homogeneous HNP P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, the unique solutions of the Cauchy problems E​q.(3.5)Eq.\,(\ref{Cauchy-5}) and E​q.(2.8)Eq.\,(\ref{Cauchy-2}) must be a polynomial in (z,t)(z,t) and the exponential of a polynomial (z,t)(z,t), respectively.

Since it has been proved by Wang [Wa] that the Jacobian conjecture holds for polynomial maps F⁡(z)F(z) of deg⁡F⁡(z)≤2\deg F(z)\leq 2, hence Conjecture 3.3 is true for d≤3d\leq 3. For more discussion on relationships of HNP’s and the Jacobian conjecture, see Section 7.

Next we give two different proofs for the following uniform formula for the powers Qtk​(z)Q_{t}^{k}(z) (k≥1)(k\geq 1) of the deformed inversion pairs Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of HNS P⁡(z)P(z).

Theorem 3.4.

Suppose P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 is HN. Then, for any k≥1k\geq 1, we have

In particular, for any m≥1m\geq 1,

(3.9) Q[m]​(z)=12m−1​m!​(m−1)!​Δm−1​Pm​(z).\displaystyle Q_{[m]}(z)=\frac{1}{2^{m-1}m!(m-1)!}\Delta^{m-1}P^{m}(z).

(3.10) exp⁡(t2​s​Δ)​exp⁡(s​P)=∑k=0∞tk(2​s)k​k!​Δk​exp⁡(s​P).\displaystyle\exp(\frac{t}{2s}\Delta)\exp(sP)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{k}}{(2s)^{k}k!}\Delta^{k}\exp(sP).

Corollary 3.6.

Note that, by setting s=1s=1 in Eq. (3.11), we have the following formula.

(3.14) exp⁡(Qt)=exp⁡(t2​Δ)​exp⁡(P).\displaystyle\exp(Q_{t})=\exp({\frac{t}{2}\Delta})\exp(P).

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 such that Δ2​P​(z)=0\Delta^{2}P(z)=0, we have Q~t​(z)=0\widetilde{Q}_{t}(z)=0, or in other words, Qt​(z)=P​(z)Q_{t}(z)=P(z).

4. A Criterion for Hessian nilpotency

Let a={aI|I∈ℕn,|I|≥2}a=\{a_{I}|I\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n},\,|I|\geq 2\} be a set of variables which commute with each other. Let P⁡(z)=∑I∈ℕnaI​zIP(z)=\sum_{I\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}a_{I}z^{I} be the universal formal power series in zz with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2. We will also view P⁡(z)P(z) as a formal power series in zz with coefficients in ℂ⁡[a]{\mathbb{C}}[a], i.e. P​(z)∈ℂ​[a]​[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[a][[z]].

For any m≥1m\geq 1, we set

(4.1) um​(P)\displaystyle u_{m}(P) =Tr Hesm​(P),\displaystyle=\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes}^{m}(P),
(4.2) vm​(P)\displaystyle v_{m}(P) =Δm​Pm.\displaystyle=\Delta^{m}P^{m}.

In this section, we prove a general theorem, Theorem 4.1, about a relation between {um​(P)|m≥1}\{u_{m}(P)|m\geq 1\} and {vm​(P)|m≥1}\{v_{m}(P)|m\geq 1\}. Consequently, we get a criterion for Hessian nilpotency of formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] in terms of certain vanishing properties of {Δm​Pm​(z)|m≥1}\{\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)|m\geq 1\}.

Let P​(z)∈ℂ​[a]​[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[a][[z]], {um​(P)|m≥1}\{u_{m}(P)|m\geq 1\} and {vm​(P)|m≥1}\{v_{m}(P)|m\geq 1\} be defined as above.

For any k≥1k\geq 1, we define 𝒰k​(P){\mathcal{U}}_{k}(P) (resp. 𝒱k​(P){\mathcal{V}}_{k}(P)) to be the ideal in ℂ​[a]​[[z]]{\mathbb{C}}[a][[z]] generated by {um​(P)|1≤m≤k}\{u_{m}(P)|1\leq m\leq k\} (resp. {vm​(P)|1≤m≤k}\{v_{m}(P)|1\leq m\leq k\}) and all their partial derivatives of any order. For convenience, we also set 𝒰0​(P)=𝒱0​(P)=0{\mathcal{U}}_{0}(P)={\mathcal{V}}_{0}(P)=0.

The first main result of this subsection is the following theorem.

Theorem 4.1.

For any k≥1k\geq 1, 𝒰k​(P)=𝒱k​(P){\mathcal{U}}_{k}(P)={\mathcal{V}}_{k}(P) as ideals in ℂ​[a]​[[z]]{\mathbb{C}}[a][[z]].

One immediate consequence of Theorem 4.1 is the following corollary.

For any k≥1k\geq 1, we define 𝒰~k​(P)\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}_{k}(P) (resp. 𝒱~k​(P)\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{k}(P)) to be the ideal in ℂ⁡[a]{\mathbb{C}}[a] generated by all coefficients of {um​(P)|1≤m≤k}\{u_{m}(P)|1\leq m\leq k\} (resp. {vm​(P)|1≤m≤k}\{v_{m}(P)|1\leq m\leq k\}).

Corollary 4.2.
11 1 Professor David Wright [Wr3] recently informed the author that he has obtained a different proof for this result.

For any k≥1k\geq 1, 𝒰~k​(P)=𝒱~k​(P)\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}_{k}(P)=\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{k}(P) as ideals in ℂ⁡[a]{\mathbb{C}}[a].

From Theorem 4.1 or Corollary 4.2, it is easy to see that we have the following criteria for Hessian nilpotency of formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]].

Theorem 4.3.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, the following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

  2. (2)

    Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

  3. (3)

    Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n.

Proof:  By Theorem 4.1 or Corollary 4.2, we have, for any fixed k≥1k\geq 1, Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 (1≤m≤k)(1\leq m\leq k) if and only if Tr​Hesm​(P)=0\text{Tr}\,\text{Hes}^{m}(P)=0 (1≤m≤k)(1\leq m\leq k). Then, the theorem follows directly from the following facts in linear algebra, namely, for any n×nn\times n matrix A∈Mn​(ℂ)A\in M_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), AA is nilpotent if and only if Tr ​Am=0\text{Tr\,}A^{m}=0 (m≥1)(m\geq 1), and if and only if Tr ​Am=0\text{Tr\,}A^{m}=0 (1≤m≤n)(1\leq m\leq n).  □\Box

Besides the criteria in Theorem 4.3, we believe the following one is also true.

Conjecture 4.4.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2. If Δm​Pm​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)=0 for m>>0m>>0, then P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

In the rest of this subsection, we fix the universal formal power series P⁡(z)=∑I∈ℕnaI​zIP(z)=\sum_{I\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}a_{I}z^{I} with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 and give a proof for Theorem 4.1. Note that all results proved in the previous sections also hold for formal power series over the ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-algebra ℂ⁡[a]{\mathbb{C}}[a]. In particular, they hold for our universal formal power series P​(z)∈ℂ​[a]​[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[a][[z]].

5. Hessian Nilpotent Polynomials

In this section, we first derive in Subsection 5.1 a criterion for Hessian nilpotency of homogeneous polynomials by using a fundamental theorem (See Theorem 5.2) of harmonic polynomials. We then give in Subsection 5.2 some examples of HNP’s (Hessian nilpotent polynomials) and HNS (Hessian nilpotent formal power series).

5.1. A Criterion for Hessian Nilpotency of Homogeneous Harmonic Polynomials

For any n≥1n\geq 1, we let X⁡(ℂn)X({\mathbb{C}}^{n}) or simply XX denote the affine variety defined by ∑i=1nzi2=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}=0. For any d≥0d\geq 0, we denoted by Vd​(z)V_{d}(z) the vector space of homogeneous polynomials in zz of degree d≥0d\geq 0. For any α∈ℂn\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, we denote by hα​(z)h_{\alpha}(z) the linear function <α,z><\alpha,z> of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}.

The following identities are almost trivial but very useful for our later arguments. So we formulate them as a lemma without giving proofs.

Lemma 5.1.

(a)(a) For any α∈ℂn\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} and m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(5.1) Hes ​(hαm)​(z)=m⁡(m−1)​hαm−2​(z)​α⋅αt\displaystyle\text{Hes\,}(h_{\alpha}^{m})(z)=m(m-1)h_{\alpha}^{m-2}(z)\,\alpha\cdot\alpha^{t}

For any homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, we have

(5.3) P⁡(z)=∑i=1kci​hαid​(z)\displaystyle P(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}h_{\alpha_{i}}^{d}(z)

for some ci∈ℂc_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}} and αi∈X⁡(ℂn)\alpha_{i}\in X({\mathbb{C}}^{n}) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k).

for some αi∈X⁡(ℂn)\alpha_{i}\in X({\mathbb{C}}^{n}) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k).

A more general construction is as follows.

Note that, by setting wi=ziw_{i}=z_{i} and βi∈X⁡(ℂ2​n)\beta_{i}\in X({\mathbb{C}}^{2n}) such that hαi​(u,v)=ui+−1​vih_{\alpha_{i}}(u,v)=u_{i}+\sqrt{-1}v_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), we have Ug​(u,v)=Pg​(u,v)U_{g}(u,v)=P_{g}(u,v).

6. More Properties of HN Polynomials

In this section, we derive more properties of HNS (Hessian nilpotent formal power series) and HNP’s (Hessian nilpotent polynomials). We prove an identity in Proposition 6.1 and an equivalence of certain vanishing properties in Theorem 6.2 of {ΔkPm(z)|k,m≥1}\{\Delta^{k}P^{m}(z)|k,m\geq 1\} for HNS P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]. In Subsection 6.3, we study an isotropic property of {ΔkPm(z)|k,m≥1}\{\Delta^{k}P^{m}(z)|k,m\geq 1\} for homogeneous HNP’s P⁡(z)P(z).

6.1. An Identity of HN Formal Power Series

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] be a HNS. For any k≥0k\geq 0 and α≥1\alpha\geq 1, we set

(6.1) uk,α​(P)=α!2k​k!​(k+α)!​Δk​Pk+α.\displaystyle u_{k,\alpha}(P)=\frac{\alpha!}{2^{k}k!(k+\alpha)!}\Delta^{k}P^{k+\alpha}.
Proposition 6.1.

For any α,β≥1\alpha,\beta\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

(6.2) um,α+β​(P)=∑k+l=mk,l≥0uk,α​(P)​ul,β​(P).\displaystyle u_{m,\alpha+\beta}(P)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l=m\\ k,l\geq 0\end{subarray}}u_{k,\alpha}(P)u_{l,\beta}(P).

More explicitly, we have

(6.3) Δm​Pm+α+β=(α+βα)−1​∑k+l=mk,l≥0(mk)​(m+α+βk+α)​(Δk​Pk+α)​(Δl​Pl+β).\displaystyle\Delta^{m}P^{m+\alpha+\beta}=\binom{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha}^{-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l=m\\ k,l\geq 0\end{subarray}}\binom{m}{k}\binom{m+\alpha+\beta}{k+\alpha}(\Delta^{k}P^{k+\alpha})(\Delta^{l}P^{l+\beta}).

Proof:  First, it is easy to see that Eq. (6.3) follows directly from Eq. (6.2) and (6.1). So we only need prove Eq. (6.2).

By Eq. (3.8) and (6.1), we have

(6.4) Qtγ​(z)=∑m=0∞um,γ​(P)​tm\displaystyle Q_{t}^{\gamma}(z)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}u_{m,\gamma}(P)t^{m}

for any γ≥1\gamma\geq 1. By comparing the coefficients of tmt^{m} of both sides of the equation Qtα+β​(z)=Qtα​(z)​Qtβ​(z)Q_{t}^{\alpha+\beta}(z)=Q_{t}^{\alpha}(z)Q_{t}^{\beta}(z), we see that Eq. (6.2) holds.  □\Box

6.2. A Vanishing Property of HN Formal Power Series

Theorem 6.2.

For any HNS P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]], the following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    For any k≥1k\geq 1, Δm​Pm+k=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+k}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

  2. (2)

    There exists k0≥1k_{0}\geq 1, Δm​Pm+k0=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+k_{0}}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

  3. (3)

    Δm​Pm+1=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

Proof:  (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2) is trivial. To show (2)⇒(3)(2)\Rightarrow(3), we assume that Δm​Pm+k0=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+k_{0}}=0 when m>M0m>M_{0} for some M0≥1M_{0}\geq 1. For any m>M0+k0−1m>M_{0}+k_{0}-1, we have

Δm​Pm+1=Δk0−1​(Δm−k0+1​P(m−k0+1)+k0)=0.\displaystyle\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=\Delta^{k_{0}-1}(\Delta^{m-k_{0}+1}P^{(m-k_{0}+1)+k_{0}})=0.

Hence (3)(3) holds in this case.

Now we consider (3)⇒(1)(3)\Rightarrow(1). Since P⁡(z)P(z) is HN, Eq. (3.8) in Theorem 3.4 holds for any k≥1k\geq 1. In particular, Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) is a polynomial in tt with coefficients in ℂ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{C}}[[z]] by our assumption of (3)(3). Therefore, for any k≥1k\geq 1, Qtk​(z)Q^{k}_{t}(z) is also a polynomial in tt with coefficients in ℂ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]. By Eq. (3.8) again, we see that (1)(1) holds.  □\Box

We believe that Theorem 7.2 is still true without the Hessian nilpotency condition. Actually, if Conjecture 4.4 is true, it is certainly the case. More precisely, suppose that one of the statements, say (3)(3), of Theorem 7.2 holds for some P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]. Then we have

Δm+1​Pm+1=Δ⁡(Δm​Pm+1)=0\displaystyle\Delta^{m+1}P^{m+1}=\Delta(\Delta^{m}P^{m+1})=0

when m>>0m>>0. If Conjecture 4.4 is true, then P⁡(z)P(z) is HN. Hence all other statements of Theorem 7.2 also hold.

Later we will show in Theorem 7.2 that the Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to saying that one of the statements in Theorem 6.2 holds for HNP’s P⁡(z)P(z).

6.3. Isotropic Properties of Homogeneous HN Polynomials

For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, we set Di=∂∂ziD_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}} and D=(D1,D2,⋯,Dn)D=(D_{1},D_{2},\cdots,D_{n}). We define a ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear map {⋅,⋅}:ℂ⁡[z]×ℂ⁡[z]→ℂ⁡[z]\{\cdot,\cdot\}:{\mathbb{C}}[z]\times{\mathbb{C}}[z]\to{\mathbb{C}}[z] by setting {f,g}=f⁡(D)​g​(z)\{f,g\}=f(D)g(z) for any f,g∈ℂ⁡[z]f,g\in{\mathbb{C}}[z]. The ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear map {⋅,⋅}\{\cdot,\cdot\} defined above is closely related with the following commonly used Hermitian inner product of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z]. See, for example, [ABR], [H] and [KR].

(⋅,⋅):ℂ⁡[z]×ℂ⁡[z]\displaystyle(\cdot,\cdot):{\mathbb{C}}[z]\times{\mathbb{C}}[z] →ℂ,\displaystyle\to{\mathbb{C}},
(f,g)\displaystyle(f,\quad g)\quad →(f​(D)​g¯)​(0),\displaystyle\to(f(D)\bar{g})(0),

where, g¯​(z)=∑I∈ℕna¯𝐬​z𝐬\bar{g}(z)=\sum_{I\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}\bar{a}_{\bf s}z^{\bf s} if g⁡(z)=∑I∈ℕna𝐬​z𝐬g(z)=\sum_{I\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}a_{\bf s}z^{\bf s}. In particular, for any homogeneous polynomials f,g∈ℂ⁡[z]f,g\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] of the same degree, we have {f,g¯}=(f,g)\{f,\bar{g}\}=(f,g).

Actually, the Hermitian inner product (⋅,⋅)(\cdot,\cdot) plays an very important role in the study of classical harmonic polynomials (See [ABR] and [H].). Due to the connection of {⋅,⋅}\{\cdot,\cdot\} with the Hermitian inner product (⋅,⋅)(\cdot,\cdot) described above, we refer to the properties of HNP’s derived in this subsection as certain isotropic properties.

The main result of this subsection is the following theorem.

7. Vanishing Conjectures of HN Polynomials

In this section, we propose some conjectures on certain vanishing properties of polynomials {ΔkPm(z)|m,k≥1 and m>k}\{\Delta^{k}P^{m}(z)|m,k\geq 1\text{ and }m>k\} for HNP’s (Hessian Nilpotent polynomials) P⁡(z)P(z). We also show that these so-called vanishing conjectures are equivalent to the well-known Jacobian conjecture.

Conjecture 7.1.

(Vanishing Conjecture )
For any HN (not necessarily homogeneous)(\text{not necessarily homogeneous}) polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, its deformed inversion pair Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) is a polynomial in both tt and zz. More precisely, Δk​Pk+1=0\Delta^{k}P^{k+1}=0 when k>>0k>>0.

Theorem 7.2.

The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    The vanishing conjecture for homogeneous HNP of degree d=4d=4.

  2. (2)

    The vanishing conjecture for homogeneous HNP of degree d≥2d\geq 2.

  3. (3)

    The vanishing conjecture.

  4. (4)

    The Jacobian conjecture.

Proof:  First, it is easy to see that (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1), (3)⇒(1)(3)\Rightarrow(1) and (3)⇒(2)(3)\Rightarrow(2) are trivial. By the gradient reduction in [BE1] and the homogeneous reduction in [BCW], [Y] on the Jacobian conjecture, we know that the Jacobian conjecture will be true if it is true for polynomial maps F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) with P⁡(z)P(z) being homogeneous HNP of degree d=4d=4. Therefore, (4)⇔(1)(4)\Leftrightarrow(1) follows directly from Eq. (3.8) in Theorem 3.4. Hence we only need show (4)⇒(3)(4)\Rightarrow(3).

Now we assume the Jacobian conjecture and let P⁡(z)P(z) be a HNP of degree d≥2d\geq 2. Let Ft(z)=z−t∇P(z)F_{t}(z)=z-t\nabla P(z) and Gt(z)=z+t∇Qt(z)G_{t}(z)=z+t\nabla Q_{t}(z) as before. Consider the formal map U⁡(z,t)=(Ft​(z),t)U(z,t)=(F_{t}(z),t) from ℂn+1→ℂn+1{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{n+1}. It is easy to check that the Jacobian of the map U⁡(z,t)U(z,t) with respect to (z,t)(z,t) is also identically equal to 11 and the formal inverse V⁡(z,t)V(z,t) is given by V⁡(z,t)=(Gt​(z),t)V(z,t)=(G_{t}(z),t). Since we have assumed the Jacobian conjecture, V⁡(z,t)V(z,t) must be a polynomial in (z,t)(z,t). Hence so is Gt​(z)G_{t}(z). By Eq. (3.8) again, we see that Δm​Pm+1​(z)\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z) must vanish when m>>0m>>0.  □\Box

Next, by using the upper bound given in [BCW], Corollary 1.41.4, for the degrees of inverse maps of polynomial automorphisms of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, we show that Conjecture 7.1 for homogeneous HNP’s can actually be reformulated more precisely as follows.

Conjecture 7.3.

(Homogeneous Vanishing Conjecture)
For any homogeneous HNP P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, we have

  1. (1)

    Δm​Pm+1=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=0 for any m>α[n,d]:=1d−2​((d−1)n−1−(d−1))m>\alpha_{[n,d]}:=\frac{1}{d-2}((d-1)^{n-1}-(d-1)).

  2. (2)

    For any k≥1k\geq 1, Δm​Pm+k=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+k}=0 for any m>k​α[n,d]m>k\alpha_{[n,d]}.

Proposition 7.4.

(a)(a) For any homogeneous HNP P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, the statements (1)(1) and (2)(2) in Conjecture 7.3 are equivalent.

(b)(b) Conjecture 7.3 for d≥2d\geq 2 and Conjecture 7.3 for d=4d=4 are both equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture.

Proof:  (a)(a) First, (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1) is trivial. Now we show that (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2). By Eq. (3.8) with k=1k=1, we see that the degree degt⁡Qt​(z)\deg_{t}Q_{t}(z) of Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) with respect to tt is less or equal to αn,d\alpha_{n,d}, i.e. degt⁡Qt​(z)≤α[n,d]\deg_{t}Q_{t}(z)\leq\alpha_{[n,d]}. Therefore, for any k≥1k\geq 1, we have, degt⁡Qtk​(z)≤k​α[n,d]\deg_{t}Q^{k}_{t}(z)\leq k\alpha_{[n,d]}. By Eq. (3.8) again, we see that (2)(2) holds for any k≥1k\geq 1.

(b)(b) By theorem 7.2, it is easy to see that Conjecture 7.3 for d≥2d\geq 2 or Conjecture 7.3 with d=4d=4 implies the Jacobian conjecture. Therefore it will be enough to show that the Jacobian conjecture implies Conjecture 7.3. By Corollary 1.41.4 in [BCW], we know that, for any polynomial automorphism F⁡(z)F(z) of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with deg⁡F⁡(z)=d−1\deg F(z)=d-1, deg⁡G⁡(z)≤(d−1)n−1\deg G(z)\leq(d-1)^{n-1}. By applying this result to the polynomial automorphism F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) and its inverse G​(z)=z−∇Q​(z)G(z)=z-\nabla Q(z), we get deg⁡Q⁡(z)≤(d−1)n−1+1\deg Q(z)\leq(d-1)^{n-1}+1. Furthermore, by Eq. (3.8) with k=1k=1 and the fact deg⁡Δm​Pm+1​(z)=(m+1)​d−2​m\deg\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=(m+1)d-2m (m≥1)(m\geq 1), we get Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 if

(m+1)​d−2​m>(d−1)n−1+1.\displaystyle(m+1)d-2m>(d-1)^{n-1}+1.

By separating mm from the inequality above, we get Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 whenever m>α[n,d]m>\alpha_{[n,d]}.  □\Box

Finally, by translating certain known results on the Jacobian conjecture, we know that the vanishing conjectures, Conjecture 7.1 or 7.3, are true for the following cases.

  1. ∙\bullet

    S. Wang [Wa] proved that the Jacobian conjecture holds for any polynomial map F⁡(z)F(z) of deg⁡F⁡(z)≤2\deg F(z)\leq 2. Hence Conjecture 7.1 and 7.3 hold for any HNP P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≤3d\leq 3.

  2. ∙\bullet

    For any symmetric polynomial map F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) with o⁡(H⁡(z))≥2o(H(z))\geq 2 and J​H​(z)JH(z) nilpotent, A. van den Essen and S. Washburn [EW] showed that the Jacobian conjecture holds when n≤4n\leq 4 and H⁡(z)H(z) is homogeneous. Later, M. de Bondt and A. van den Essen [BE2]-[BE4] further proved that the Jacobian conjecture holds either n≤4n\leq 4 without H⁡(z)H(z) being homogeneous, or n=5n=5 with H⁡(z)H(z) being homogeneous. ((For an exposition discussion on these results, see [BE5].)). From the results above, we see that, Conjecture 7.1 has an affirmative answer when n≤4n\leq 4, and Conjecture 7.3 is true when n≤5n\leq 5.

  3. ∙\bullet

    By Theorem 4.14.1 in [EW] and similar arguments there, it is easy to show that the only HNP’s ((not necessarily homogeneous)) P⁡(z)∈ℝ⁡[z]P(z)\in{\mathbb{R}}[z] (o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2)(o(P(z))\geq 2) with real coefficients are P⁡(z)=0P(z)=0. Hence, Conjecture 7.1 and 7.3 hold trivially in this case.

  4. ∙\bullet

    Recently, D. Wright [Wr1] showed that the Jacobian conjecture holds for any symmetric polynomial map F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) with H⁡(z)H(z) homogeneous and J​H3​(z)=0JH^{3}(z)=0. Hence Conjecture 7.3 holds for any homogeneous HNP P⁡(z)P(z) with Hes 3​(P​(z))=0\text{Hes\,}^{3}(P(z))=0.

Furthermore, by Corollary 3.9, we also know that Conjecture 7.1 holds for any HNP P⁡(z)P(z) such that Δ​P2​(z)=0\Delta P^{2}(z)=0. In particular, it is true for HNP’s constructed by Eq.(5.13) and Eq.(5.14).
